questions.q: What does setting requires_grad=True on a tensor actually do?
options: It converts the tensor to a NumPy array
It turns on tracking so PyTorch records the operations used to produce derived tensors, building a computational graph
It moves the tensor to the GPU
It forces the tensor to use float16 precision
questions.explain: requires_grad=True opts a tensor into autograd tracking: every operation applied to it (or tensors derived from it) is recorded via grad_fn, forming the computational graph that .backward() later walks.

questions.q: Why does .backward() typically need to be called on a scalar tensor (like a loss)?
options: Because non-scalar tensors cannot have a grad_fn
Because without a scalar, PyTorch needs an explicit gradient argument to know how to weight each output element during the chain rule
Because scalars compute faster on GPU
Because .backward() only exists on torch.float64 tensors
questions.explain: Calling .backward() with no arguments implicitly uses a gradient of 1.0, which only makes sense for a scalar. For non-scalar outputs you must supply a gradient tensor matching its shape, so training loops reduce the loss to a single number first.

questions.q: A training loop omits optimizer.zero_grad(). What happens across iterations?
options: Nothing; .grad is automatically reset before every backward() call
The model raises a RuntimeError immediately
Gradients from previous iterations accumulate into .grad instead of being replaced, corrupting the update direction
Only the first layer's gradients are affected
questions.explain: Gradients accumulate by design (useful for some advanced patterns), so without zeroing them each iteration, stale gradients from earlier batches silently add to the current ones.

questions.q: When should you wrap code in torch.no_grad()?
options: Whenever you want faster, lower-memory execution for code that doesn't need gradients, such as evaluation or inference
Only when running on a GPU
Whenever you want to permanently delete a tensor's gradient history
Before calling .backward() on the loss
questions.explain: torch.no_grad() is a context manager that disables graph construction for the code inside it, which is appropriate for evaluation/inference and manual parameter updates where gradient tracking would waste memory or cause errors.

questions.q: What is the difference between tensor.detach() and torch.no_grad()?
options: They are identical in every way
detach() moves a tensor to CPU; no_grad() moves it to GPU
detach() returns a new tensor sharing the same data but disconnected from the graph; no_grad() is a context manager that prevents graph-building for a block of code
detach() deletes the tensor; no_grad() only pauses tracking temporarily
questions.explain: detach() gives you one tensor with gradient history removed, useful for pulling a value out of the graph. no_grad() instead scopes an entire block of code so nothing inside it builds graph history in the first place.
